newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian leader vows free ballot after bloodshed.
newsitem.headline: Algerian leader vows free ballot after bloodshed.

text.p: Algerian President Liamine Zeroual on Wednesday promised free and fair local elections would be held in October to cement democracy and bring stability to the country convulsed by years of bloodshed.

"I'm convinced that the Algerian people, who are putting much hope on the elections, will once again live up to this event which will help bring the definitive rupture with the situation of instability," he said.
Zeroual was quoted by the official Algerian news agency APS as addressing opposition party and human rights group representatives as they were sworn in as a multi-party watchdog for the elections.

He added: "We understand that the setting up of the national independent committee to supervise the local elections will make sure that all possible conditions for a transparent and regular poll are met."
The local ballot was cited on Wednesday by the cabinet as one reason why the government had to adopt a minibudget to meet soaring spending on the top of the initial budget for 1997.
The elections are to enable Algerian voters to elect local authorities in the country's 48 cities and some 1,500 towns and villagers.

Many are run by government officials, appointed after elected representatives from the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), were expelled after being accused of supporting a network of militants seeking to install a purist Islamist state.
The new councils, particularly in villages and isolated areas, face the daunting task of tackling widespread killings of villagers and residents of isolated communities.
The election will also complete the shape of the Algerian parliament after last month's general election of a 380-member National Assembly (lower house).
Two-thirds of a new upper house, the Council of the Nation, will be voted by those elected to local authorities in the October 23 ballot.
The president will select the last third of the 144-member Council which with the National Assembly forms the parliament.
Zeroual, in his speech, made no comments on the increased massacres of villagers in hamlets south of Algiers in which more than 170 people have perished in the past week.
On Tuesday, a bomb killed two girls south of Algiers as bereaved villagers in a nearby hamlet buried some 50 relatives slaughtered by rebels on Sunday, an Algerian newspaper said.
The home-made bomb exploded by a house near Chrea, about 50 km (about 30 miles) south of Algiers, killing the two girls aged 10 and 12 years, said El Watan newspaper on Wednesday.
About 60,000 people have been killed since early 1992 when authorities cancelled a general election in which the FIS had taken a commanding lead.

Earlier this month, FIS chief Abassi Madani was freed half way through a 12-year term for threatening state security. He vowed shortly after his release that he and his supporters would strive to stop the bloodshed.
Newspapers said the latest massacres were in retaliation for a military offensive on guerrilla strongholds in the past three weeks in which up to 300 rebels were killed and scores captured.

According to the newspapers, the rebels belonged to cells of the Armed Islamic Group (GIA) who had gathered to plot strategy when they were trapped. Algerian officials blame the GIA for most of the massacres of civilians in isolated villages.
